Barclays backs Euronext on bond growth, turns cautious on Deutsche Boerse
sum: Investing.com — Barclays повысил рейтинг биржевого оператора Euronext с «равновесного» до «избыточного» и повысил целевую цену до 210 евро со 160 евро, заявив, что рост его бизнеса по торговле государственными облигациями недооценен.

Barclays сократил вес биржевого оператора Deutsche Boerse до «равного веса» с «избыточного», поскольку его акции выросли почти на 50% за последние 12 месяцев и теперь торгуются по неизменной целевой цене Barclays в 320 евро.

Рейтинг «выше рынка» означает, что Barclays ожидает, что акции превысят среднюю доходность европейских диверсифицированных финансовых компаний, которые он охватывает, за 12 месяцев; «равный вес» означает соответствие этому среднему значению.
Котировки Euronext 12 ноября закрылись на уровне €166,20. Новая цель Barclays, самая высокая на бирже, предполагает почти 30%-ный потенциал роста.

Barclays ожидает, что выручка Euronext с фиксированной доходностью будет расти на 24% в год с 2026 по 2028 год до 344 миллионов евро с 224 миллионов евро, что он назвал ключевым фактором прибыли выше консенсуса. Фиксированный доход составляет около 10% выручки группы.

Рост опирается на МТС, электронную торговую платформу Euronext, которая обслуживает около 70% электронных торгов между дилерами европейскими государственными облигациями, согласно новым данным по европейскому рынку облигаций.
Этот тип торговли вырос примерно до 45% объема государственных облигаций с примерно 15-20% в конце 2022 и 2023 годов, достигнув примерно 2,3 триллиона евро в сентябре.

Barclays' IBIT Stake Jumps 48% in Q3; Banks' Share of Bitcoin ETF Holdings Rises to 4.9%
sum: According to a Cointelegraph report, Barclays (BCS.US) significantly added to its position in BlackRock's (BLK.US) iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT.US) in the third quarter, holding about 3.94 million shares as of September 30, up about 48% from 2.66 million shares at the end of June. Based on its 13F filing submitted on November 6, the position was worth about $187 million (approximately NT$6.1 billion), compared with just $88.5 million (approximately NT$2.9 billion) at the end of the second quarter.

The British banking giant's move is not an isolated case. Citigroup (C.US) disclosed over the same period that it had established a new position in Fidelity's Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC.US) worth about $119 million (approximately NT$3.9 billion), while raising its IBIT holdings from about 347,000 shares to about 521,000 shares, an increase of roughly 50%. The two major banks' simultaneous expansion of spot bitcoin ETF exposure reflects how traditional financial institutions are incorporating crypto assets into their existing portfolios through regulated, compliant channels.

It is worth noting that the jump in the market value of Barclays' holdings stems not only from actual purchases but also from price factors. IBIT's price rose about 41% in the third quarter; in other words, a considerable portion of the book-value growth came from bitcoin's rally rather than an equivalent increase in new buying. Market participants therefore caution that to assess whether institutions are genuinely adding exposure, one should look at changes in the number of shares held rather than only at the reported dollar amounts.

The overall trend in institutional positioning is nonetheless clear. According to Bitwise statistics, among the 1,389 institutions that have filed third-quarter reports, the banking sector collectively holds about $258 million (approximately NT$8.5 billion) in spot bitcoin ETFs, accounting for 4.9% of disclosed holdings, up from $107 million (approximately NT$3.5 billion) and 3.2% in the second quarter. Total holdings across these institutions rose from $3.35 billion (approximately NT$110 billion) to $5.25 billion (approximately NT$170 billion), an increase of about 56.7%.

Barclays downgrades Maersk on negative risk-reward, shares dip
sum: Investing.com -- Barclays downgraded A.P. Moller-Maersk to Underweight from Equal Weight and slashed its price target to 17,500 Danish kroner from 25,000, saying the risk-reward has turned negative as higher investment needs weigh on free cash flow.
The change is "less about near-term earnings, which remain supported, and more about medium-term risk-reward," analyst Marco Limite wrote.

Limite gave five reasons for the downgrade. First, management said at the third quarter that "there are more opportunities today to reinvest into the business than there was just a few years ago," pointing to capex above the roughly $5 billion historical average. Lease costs should also rise in 2027, with the existing fleet at about 95% utilization, and from 2028 up to 70% of vessel delivery capex is paid in the year of delivery.

Second, buybacks have moved down the capital allocation list. A larger buyback had been one of Barclays' positive catalysts, but with capex needs rising and balance sheet flexibility a priority, Limite sees a lower chance of meaningful support.

Third, 2026 tailwinds from strong demand and supply congestion could normalize in 2027, putting pressure on rates. Limite said strong Chinese exports, driven by AI, electric vehicles and green technology, could be hit by AI-related regulation and potential EU-China trade barriers.

Fourth, investor expectations already seem to reflect a solid 2027, with only a modest earnings decline. Barclays forecasts 2027 EBITDA of $12.5 billion, $1.5 billion below 2026, and sees no significant upside risk.

Fifth, the 2028 earnings trough is moving into view. Newbuild deliveries add about 10% to industry capacity in 2027, which looks manageable, but a further 17% in 2028 "will be much harder to absorb," the analyst wrote.

Bloom Energy Lands Barclays Upgrade as Google and NTT DATA Deals Put Fuel Cells at the Heart of AI P
sum: Bloom Energy shares climbed 4.1% on Wednesday, riding a broader rebound in technology and growth stocks as investors shifted attention back to the company's fuel-cell projects with Google and NTT DATA. The advance came a day after Barclays lifted its rating on the stock from "Equal-Weight" to "Overweight," even as analyst Christine Cho trimmed her price target to $289 from $316. Cho pointed to demand that is gathering pace faster than anticipated — an upgrade in sentiment that, notably, arrived without a corresponding increase in the target price.

The rally followed a rough session for companies tied to data-center buildouts. Reuters reported a wide selloff in technology and AI-related names as investors reassessed what the previous day's Democratic midterm victories might mean for the pace of AI infrastructure spending. Bloom was caught in that downdraft before recovering.

The catalyst investors are watching most closely is Google's announcement of a $17 billion data center in Wyoming, part of whose power supply is slated to come from a fuel-cell installation Bloom is expected to equip. The project calls for 702 megawatts of fuel-cell capacity and includes CO? capture and storage — a combination that pairs electricity for the campus with a planned method for handling its emissions. Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital round out the partner list.

That pairing of power supply and carbon management sits at the center of the Bloom thesis. Its fuel cells run mainly on natural gas and generate electricity without combustion; adding carbon capture to the Wyoming project would extend that model to the emissions side of the equation. The opportunity is real, provided the plans turn into built plants.

The same caveat applies to a partnership reported Wednesday with California Resource Corporation and Carbon TerraVault. The companies will study power-generation projects with CO? capture exceeding 1 GW. For Bloom, it is another route to linking its fuel cells with emissions handling — but the arrangement is non-binding, which makes execution, not intention, the measure that matters. Firm project commitments now carry more weight than announcements.

Bloom Energy Rallies as Barclays Turns Bullish, but California Carbon Pact Remains a Blueprint
sum: Bloom Energy shares climbed 7.2% on Tuesday, extending a rally set in motion a day earlier when Barclays lifted its rating on the fuel-cell maker and the company unveiled a preliminary carbon-capture partnership in California. Monday's session had already delivered a 9.1% advance, with media reports pointing to the same two catalysts behind both moves.

The Barclays note moved Bloom to Overweight from Equal Weight, with analyst Christine Cho citing faster-than-expected demand, rising customer down payments and new delivery commitments. Yet the bank trimmed its price target to $289 from $316 — a reminder that a more favourable rating does not automatically translate into a higher valuation benchmark.

Separately, director John T. Chambers offloaded 8,828 shares on Monday at a weighted average price of $203.43, according to a mandatory filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. The transaction was executed under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan adopted on 26 February, a structure that fixes sales in advance and shields insiders from timing allegations.

Ownership disclosures also shifted. Vanguard Capital Management reported an economically attributable stake of 7.39% in a Schedule 13G filed on 30 October, with the filing naming 30 September as the event date.

The non-binding letter of intent with California Resources Corporation and its unit Carbon TerraVault covers a feasibility review of at least 1 GW of fuel-cell capacity, to be paired with carbon capture and storage in California. According to Data Center Dynamics, the concept could eventually capture and store up to 3 million tonnes of CO? annually. Both figures describe the project's potential, not capacity already in place.

Utilities, data centres and industrial customers are named as possible offtakers. The appeal of the arrangement lies in treating power supply and carbon management as a single package rather than two separate ventures — a route that could take Bloom beyond the economics of an individual fuel-cell installation. Whether that becomes a durable business depends on more than the technical concept.
California Resources Corporation has stressed that the plan hinges on definitive agreements, financing, required permits and further consents.

sum: Commerzbank has repurchased 21,268,730 of its own shares since launching the current buyback programme on 4 September, the lender disclosed on Monday. The tally, which runs through Friday, confirms the bank is still executing the plan rather than merely talking about it — a distinction that matters with third-quarter figures due on 5 November.

The most recent weekly report covers 26 to 30 October, during which 3,316,027 shares were bought back. That pace is slower than the 3,681,593 shares reported for the prior week on 26 October. Neither figure says anything about an expansion or a conclusion of the programme; they simply track how much of the existing mandate has been carried out.

Buybacks of this kind speak to how Commerzbank is deploying capital. They do not answer the question investors are really asking, which is whether the core business can stand on its own. That makes the 5 November release the more consequential date on the calendar, with the analyst call set for 09:00 and the press conference at 10:30.

Sentiment around the standalone case took a knock on 22 October, when Barclays analyst Paola Sabbione cut her price target to 41 euros and downgraded the stock from "Overweight" to "Equal Weight." The move is a counterweight to any thesis built purely on takeover speculation — though it is no forecast for the upcoming report.

Separately, the ECB last week trimmed the additional Pillar 2 capital requirement (P2R) for 2027 by 5 basis points to 2.10% of total capital. Commerzbank puts its pro-forma MDA threshold for hard core capital at 10.26% of risk-weighted assets. Lower capital requirements are not the same as higher earnings, and no fresh buyback commitment can be inferred from the combination.

On the operational side, ver.di has called employees at private banks, Commerzbank included, to regional warning strikes, with collective bargaining talks due to resume in Frankfurt on Monday. No earnings impact can be quantified from the walkout, and neither can any effect on day-to-day operations — but the dispute sharpens the question of how well the business absorbs extra costs.
The takeover question remains open. According to Reuters, UniCredit said on Friday it would keep financing German mid-sized companies even in the event of a possible acquisition.

Siemens Energy: Barclays Flags a Margin Ceiling as a 6.1% AI Slide Puts 11 November in the Spotlight
sum: Siemens Energy shares fell 6.1% on Friday, caught in a widening pullback from artificial intelligence names. For investors, the sell-off raises a question that has less to do with the share price than with the business behind it: can the company still justify expectations built on higher prices and wider margins, or do those forecasts now need trimming?

According to dpa-AFX, doubts about the profitability of multi-billion-dollar AI investments weighed on Siemens Energy alongside its peers. Media reports pointed to Intel's weaker quarterly outlook as an additional drag on AI-linked stocks. The decline is therefore best read as a reaction to the broader market backdrop rather than to any new guidance from Siemens Energy itself.

That distinction matters. A sector-wide loss of confidence can hit companies whose own expectations are unchanged — but it can equally expose assumptions that had gone unchallenged. The price move alone does not settle which reading applies.

The more specific pressure came from Barclays, which according to media reports warned of limited room for further price and margin increases in the energy technology sector. The scepticism is thus not confined to the scale of future data-centre spending. It extends to how much economic benefit suppliers can actually extract from it.

For Siemens Energy shareholders, demand and earnings quality are two separate things. Even if investment keeps flowing, the terms available to equipment makers remain an open question. The risk therefore lies not only in possible project cuts but in assumptions about profitability that may prove too optimistic.

Comments on pricing and margins will carry particular weight at the next set of results. Hard evidence could help separate industry-wide caution from the company's own trajectory. General confidence about demand, by contrast, would not fully answer the concern about a margin ceiling.

The company's ongoing share repurchase belongs in the same assessment. Siemens Energy reported the acquisition of 1,294,334 of its own shares in its latest interim disclosure, covering the period from 19 to 25 October. In total, 4,513,232 shares had been bought back under the programme by that point.

Coinbase Shares Plunge to 2-Year Low as Bitcoin Slides Under $77K and Barclays, JPMorgan Slash Targets
sum: Coinbase Global Inc (COIN) fell more than 13% in morning trading Friday to its weakest level since February 2024, as a sharp selloff in Bitcoin dragged crypto-linked equities lower and a wave of Wall Street desks trimmed their price targets on the exchange following third-quarter results.

The stock touched lows not seen in more than two years. Bitcoin (BTC) slid as much as 5.5% over 24 hours to trade near $77,000, adding fresh pressure to a sector already rattled by turmoil at rival exchange Binance.

Coinbase's quarter was a split verdict. The company reported earnings of $2.51 per share, far ahead of the $0.08 consensus tracked by Koyfin, but revenue of $1.21 billion came in just below the $1.22 billion analysts had expected.

Barclays cut its target to $120 from $149 while keeping an Underweight rating, warning that a lower revenue run rate heading into the fourth quarter and higher-than-expected costs would force a "sizeable downgrade" to near-term EBITDA estimates.

JPMorgan's Kenneth Worthington said the transaction environment remained difficult and that assigning value to Coinbase's growing prediction-markets business was a challenge. Wells Fargo, meanwhile, credited prediction markets and the USDC stablecoin with cushioning the weak crypto backdrop, though it said the quarter offered little sign of a broader acceleration.

Needham lowered its target to $197 from $205 while maintaining a Buy rating, pointing to the Binance developments as a source of market turbulence that coincided with Coinbase's report. The firm also flagged AI-driven hacking risk as a mounting concern for the sector through 2027.
Note: Target figures reflect the most recent revisions reported around Coinbase's third-quarter results. Ratings were maintained at prior levels across the desks listed.

sum: Gold prices have undergone a "reset" during the Iran war, according to Barclays, which is anticipating a rebound as an end is in sight. Though spot gold rose 3.2% on Monday to $4,375 per ounce, its highest level since June 9, it remains over 20% below its January peak of over $5,589 per ounce. The war brought the metal's safe-haven status into question, as the prospect of higher interest rates made yielding assets, like bonds, more attractive. In a note published on Monday, Barclays wrote it remains constructive on gold, saying "persistent inflation, policy uncertainty and central bank reserve diversification" would boost prices in the medium term. The analysts said these factors should "reassert themselves," as a potential peace deal between Washington and Tehran is set to be signed later this week. "Our estimates suggest gold rises by roughly 5% for every 1% increase in the level of US CPI, leaving the inflation impulse from the recent energy shock an important part of the bullish case," they wrote. Gold's fall hit mining companies Since the war, the falling price of gold has lowered miners' revenues, and the oil and gas supply shock has boosted energy prices, raising their costs. Mining companies are among the most volatile stocks , typically acting as a leveraged bet on the gold price, rising during a commodities bull run and falling further during a sell-off. But Barclays is staying selective in the sector, preferring Endeavour Mining and Hochschild as both stocks trade on cheaper multiples than Fresnillo , which the analysts say is more fully valued. The bank's global coverage holds overweight positions in Newmont Mining and Agnico Eagle Mines . That said, the bank does not anticipate an immediate comeback, as confidence in the asset among investors has ebbed. "Macro settings look set to remain a headwind for gold prices in the short term," the analysts wrote. "Gold prices are ultimately driven by investor flows, which have been negatively impacted by a range of macro factors in recent months."

Cboe Global Markets, an exchange and derivatives network, plunged more than 8% in Tuesday trading. That brought its losses for this week to more than 17%, also pacing for its largest weekly decline going back to 2020.

New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange slid more than 1% on Tuesday and is down more than 3% for the week. Nasdaq shares tumbled more than 5% in the session, dragging the stock into the red week to date.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission last week approved perpetual futures — a type of future-style contract with no expiration date — for bitcoin trading on Kalshi. This tool, known in short as "perps," is popular among retail traders abroad.

Investors are worried that the CFTC could give the green light to other asset classes to trade via perpetual futures next. That could increase competition for the traditional exchanges that have long dominated on Wall Street.
The "concern is that perps could come to equity products, and potentially displace CME/CBOE S&P products," Barclays analyst Ben Budish told clients in a Tuesday note.

items.t: Down 17% from February, do Barclays’ sub-£5 shares look a steal to me after its Q1 results?
sum: Barclays (LSE: BARC) shares are down from their 4 February one-year trade high of £5.06. This pullback looks to me to be the result of broad-based profit-taking after a strong previous run. Nonetheless, it exacerbates the existing mispricing relative to the strength of the bank’s core operations, in my view.

Indeed, the underlying business continues to generate solid earnings, maintain a strong capital position, and return substantial cash to shareholders. And that disconnect points to a potentially excellent opportunity for long-term investors to benefit if the price gravitates towards its ‘fair value’.

Asset prices, including shares, tend to move back towards a company’s ‘fair value’ over time. And to estimate fair value, discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis projects future cash flows and discounts them back to today. The more uncertain those projections are, the higher the return investors demand, increasing the discount rate.

DCF models vary depending on the assumptions used by the analyst. Using my own framework — including an 8.3% discount rate — Barclays shares appear 54% undervalued at their present price of £4.18. That implies a fair value of £9.09, more than twice the current level.
So, if the price continues to converge towards fair value, this could be a tremendous buying opportunity if those DCF assumptions hold good.

Q1 2026’s results, released on 28 April, showed group income up 6% year on year to £8.2bn. It reflected the benefit of higher net interest income, supported by lending growth across the UK and US businesses and structural hedge gains. The hedge is a long‑dated interest‑rate portfolio that smooths earnings when rates move, and it continues to support income even as margins stabilise.

Profit before tax increased 3% to £2.8bn, highlighting the resilience of the bank’s diversified model, despite a £200m impairment in the Investment Bank. This underlined the ongoing benefit of the bank’s recent shift toward fee-based rather than income-based business.

sum: Shares in DHL Group climbed 2% in early trading, following a significant upgrade from Barclays that reflects growing confidence in the logistics giant’s ability to capitalize on geopolitical disruption in the air freight sector. The upgrade marks a notable shift in analyst sentiment toward the German logistics provider, which has navigated a challenging period of mixed market expectations.

Barclays analyst Marco Limite raised his rating on DHL Group to Overweight from Equal Weight, simultaneously lifting the price target to EUR 54 from EUR 43. Limite cited escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East as a key driver behind the improved outlook, noting that disruption in the region is creating a favorable supply-demand dynamic in the air freight market that should benefit DHL’s operations.

The upgrade suggests potential upside to fiscal 2026 estimates, with Barclays anticipating that constrained air freight capacity and heightened demand for alternative routing solutions will support pricing power and volume growth for DHL’s express division. The Middle East disruption has historically led to longer flight routes, increased fuel surcharges, and tighter capacity utilization across the air freight industry, all factors that typically benefit established operators with global networks like DHL.

This positive reassessment from Barclays comes after a period of divergent analyst opinions on the stock. In November 2025, Morgan Stanley downgraded DHL Group from Overweight to Equal Weight, expressing concern that aggressive cost-cutting initiatives had masked underlying revenue weaknesses. That downgrade suggested limited upside potential and raised questions about the sustainability of earnings growth without top-line momentum.

sum: Administration of specialist lender raises concerns over underwriting standards and credit risk

Barclays is facing potential losses after the collapse of specialist UK bridging and buy-to-let lender Market Financial Solutions (MFS), intensifying scrutiny of private credit exposures linked to the mortgage market.

According to a Times report, Barclays has exposure of about £600 million to MFS through lending arrangements, although it is unclear how much of this sits on the bank’s own balance sheet or has already been provisioned. Analysts at Citi have suggested the size of the exposure justifies caution, while stressing that originating loans is not the same as ultimately holding the associated credit risk.

MFS was placed into administration this week following an application by lenders Amber Bridging and Zircon Bridging, who alleged “serious irregularities” in the firm’s finances. Insolvency practitioners from AlixPartners have been appointed as administrators.

According to court reports, chief insolvency and companies court judge Nicholas Briggs approved the administration after being told of alleged misuse of collateral securing loans to MFS, including so‑called “double pledging” of the same assets.

Share prices of several exposed lenders fell following the news, with Barclays and Santander among those seeing declines in trading as investors reassessed their risk positions in private credit and structured mortgage funding.

MFS, a prominent player in the UK bridging and specialist lending market, had earlier entered restructuring talks. At the time, founder Paresh Raja insisted the situation did “not reflect a failure of the underlying business or the quality of our assets, but rather a technical and procedural impasse that has temporarily limited our access to everyday banking facilities.”

items.t: Alphabet shares close flat after earnings beat. Here's what's happening
sum: Alphabet's shares closed largely flat on Thursday after the company beat Wall Street's expectations on earnings and revenue, with artificial intelligence spending projected to increase hugely this year.
The Google parent closed nearly 2% lower on Wednesday. After the bell, Alphabet reported fourth-quarter revenue of $113.83 billion, above the $111.43 billion estimate from analysts polled by LSEG.

Its Google Cloud division had $17.66 billion in revenue versus a forecast of $16.18 billion, according to StreetAccount. YouTube Advertising posted $11.38 billion in revenue versus the estimated $11.84 billion.

The tech giant said it would significantly increase its 2026 capital expenditure to between $175 billion and $185 billion — more than double its 2025 spend. A significant portion of capex spending would go toward investing in AI compute capacity for Google DeepMind.
Barclays analysts said in a note Thursday that Infrastructure, DeepMind and Waymo costs "weighed on overall Alphabet profitability," and will continue to do so in 2026.

"Cloud's growth is astonishing, measured by any metric: revenue, backlog, API tokens inferenced, enterprise adoption of Gemini. These metrics combined with DeepMind's progress on the model side, starts to justify the 100% increase in capex in '26," they said.
"The AI story is getting better while Search is accelerating - that's the most important take for GOOG," they added.

items.t: Barclays and Natwest set for bidding war in race to beef up wealth arms
sum: Barclays and Natwest are set for a bidding war as the banks prepare to make their play to snap up Evelyn Partners amid the race to beef up wealth management arms.
The blue-chip lenders are both gearing up to table offers of over £2bn for the London-based wealth manager.
A successful takeover would help enhance either bank’s presence in the wealth landscape, with Britain’s banking giants eager to grab a greater slice of this market.
Natwest already has a strong presence through its Coutts division whilst Barclays has doubled down on its private bank division, where total income reached £697m in the first half of 2025.
Both firms are expected to make a formal offer by Thursday, according to Sky News, with speculation also surrounding Royal Bank of Canada for a bid.

UK banks have staged major pivots towards the wealth sector in the last year as a source of reliable income as the Bank of England takes the chop to interest rates, which fell by one per cent last year.
The division offers lenders a less volatile and capital-light source of income, due to its reliance on recurring fees rather than the interest rate fluctuations that affect traditional lending.

items.t: UK Budget: At a glance
sum: Please note: The article does not constitute advice or any form of recommendation. Barclays Private Bank does not offer tax advice, and professional advice should always be sought.

After months of speculation, the UK government has finally unveiled its tax and spending plans for the year ahead. As many had expected, UK wealth holders are facing higher taxes – with the country’s tax burden to reach an all-time high of 38% in 2030-31, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)(1).
This article summarises some of the bigger decisions announced by the Chancellor today affecting wealth holders.

With meaningful UK growth yet to materialise and public spending rising, the government faced some difficult decisions at this year’s Budget. Its pre-election pledge not to raise the ‘big three’ taxes – income tax, VAT and national insurance – left fewer levers to pull.

The economic picture remains mixed. While the OBR increased its growth forecast for 2025 to 1.5%, it downgraded forecasts for subsequent years to 1.5% on average until 2030, due to falling UK productivity. Meanwhile, it uprated its inflation forecast for 2025 and 2026, to 3.5% and 2.5%, respectively.
On the positive side, the country’s fiscal deficit appears smaller than previously feared – while spending in some areas has accelerated, this has been offset by higher-than-expected revenues.

One change squarely targeted at the wealthiest was the introduction of a new annual levy on properties valued at over £2 million from 6th April 2028. This new so-called ‘mansion tax’ will come in the form of a council tax surcharge and will be charged at £2,500 for properties worth more than £2 million and £7,500 for homes worth in excess of £5 million, affecting an estimated 100,000 homeowners in total(2). The tax will be increased annually in line with CPI inflation and is estimated to raise approximately £400 million for the government each year.

items.t: UK bank shares rise after reports of budget tax reprieve
sum: UK bank shares have jumped as investors grow increasingly confident that the industry will be shielded from tax rises in Rachel Reeves’s budget this week.

Shares in some of the UK’s largest high street lenders rose more than 2% on Tuesday, after reports that the Treasury had asked the sector to issue supportive statements about the following day’s budget, raising expectations they would be spared a further levy.
Lloyds rose by 3.8%, NatWest went up 3.7% and Barclays added 2.3%.

“Reports that UK banks might get a reprieve in this week’s budget from previously floated new tax measures … underpinned the FTSE 100’s rise on Tuesday,” said Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at AJ Bell.

“It suggests that some intense lobbying by the industry has paid off, although U-turns have been a theme in UK politics for some time so banking boardrooms may not breathe a full sigh of relief until Rachel Reeves has sat down tomorrow afternoon.”

Speculation over potential bank tax rises has been swirling for months, having been revived in August when the IPPR thinktank argued that Reeves should levy a new bank tax to claw back money that commercial lenders earn from the Bank of England as result of an emergency economic policy known as quantitative easing put in place after the 2008 financial crisis.

The banking industry lobbied hard against a tax increase, arguing that banks in the UK were paying a total tax rate of about 45.8% when employment taxes and VAT were taken into account. That compared with a 38.6% rate in Frankfurt and 27.9% in New York.

Lloyds and Natwest shares fall in ‘perfect combination’ of fears
sum: Lloyds and Natwest shares were among the top fallers on the FTSE 100 index on Friday as a combination of fears weighed upon City stocks.
The FTSE 350 bank index lost 2.17 per cent over the course of the day amid a widespread sell off across the blue-chip index.
Lloyds Banking Group – which is often seen as an informal barometer for the UK economy due to its domestic focus – dropped nearly three per cent to 91.60p.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, told City AM: “UK banks find themselves hit by a perfect combination of global growth worries and UK-specific concerns around the Budget.”
It comes as jitters raced through UK markets following reports that Rachel Reeves has scrapped her plans to raise income tax in the forthcoming Autumn Budget.
The Chancellor was poised to hike income tax by 2p whilst cutting national insurance by the same amount in a move that would break Labour’s pledge to not raise taxes on ‘working people.’
But now the first set of Budget proposals sent to the UK fiscal watchdog – including an income tax increase – have been kicked to the curb, effectively sending Reeves back to the drawing board.
